table.text: In the Rydell et al. (2007) paradigm, participants were introduced to a novel target named Bob and learned about him via an impression formation procedure relying on valenced behavioral statements.
table.formatted: In the <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref> paradigm, participants were introduced to a novel target named Bob and learned about him via an impression formation procedure relying on valenced behavioral statements.

table.text: A total of 598 participants were recruited from the study pools at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Yale University, and Williams College.

Participants were excluded from analyses if they (a) did not complete the Implicit Association Test (IAT), which served as the key dependent measure (n = 2), or (b) had response latencies below 300 ms on 10% or more of IAT trials, indicating inattention (Greenwald et al., 2003; n = 1).
table.formatted: Participants were excluded from analyses if they (a) did not complete the Implicit Association Test (IAT), which served as the key dependent measure (n = 2), or (b) had response latencies below 300 ms on 10% or more of IAT trials, indicating inattention <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Greenwald et al., 2003</ref>; n = 1).

table.text: Participants were randomly assigned to one of six between-participant conditions, which determined the number of counterattitudinal (CA) statements to which they were exposed in the second part of the learning phase: (a) 0 CA (n = 101), (b) 20 CA (n = 96), (c) 40 CA (n = 101), (d) 60 CA (n = 108), (e) 80 CA (n = 102), and (f) 100 CA (n = 87).
Finally, participants completed some exploratory items and some basic demographic items.
On the first 100 trials, participants were exposed to 50 positive and 50 negative behavioral statements.

In the 0 CA condition, which served as a control condition, participants were exposed to 100 neutral behavioral statements, half of which were randomly assigned to be characteristic and half uncharacteristic of Bob.

In the remaining conditions, participants were first exposed to a number of CA statements (in one block), followed by a number of neutral statements to ensure that all participants completed the same number of trials.
For example, in the 60 CA condition, participants were first exposed to 30 uncharacteristic positive and 30 characteristic negative statements, followed by 40 neutral statements.
Finally, in block 5 (second critical block; 20 trials), participants completed a combined sorting task opposite of the one they had completed in block 3.
A total of 499 participants were recruited from the study pools at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Yale University, and Williams College.
Participants were excluded from analyses if they (a) did not complete the IAT (n = 3) or (b) had response latencies below 300 ms on 10% or more of IAT trials (n = 1).

Participants were randomly assigned to one of seven between-participant conditions, which determined the amount of counterattitudinal information to which they were exposed in the second part of the learning phase: (a) control (n = 73), (b) 20 CA (n = 68), (c) 40 CA (n = 67), (d) 60 CA (n = 77), (e) 80 CA (n = 68), (f) 100 CA (n = 71), and (g) 1 CA (n = 71).
To ensure appropriate retention of the newly presented information, participants were required to read each statement for at least 30 seconds before they were able to proceed to the next screen.

In the 20 CA, 40 CA, 60 CA, 80 CA, and 100 CA conditions, participants were exposed to a number of counterattitudinal behavioral statements following the same trial structure as part 1 of the learning phase.

For example, in the 60 CA condition, participants were exposed to 30 uncharacteristic positive and 30 characteristic negative statements about the experimental target, along with 12 characteristic neutral statements about the control target.
Participants completed the explicit evaluation items both for the control target (Cronbach's α = .98) and the experimental target (Cronbach's α = .93), in randomized order.

Participants were asked to indicate (a) the percentage of positive statements about Bob that were true in part 1 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (b) the percentage of negative statements about Bob that were true in part 1 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (c) the percentage of neutral statements about Bob in part 1 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (d) the percentage of positive statements about Bob that were true in part 2 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (e) the percentage of negative statements about Bob that were true in part 2 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (f) the percentage of neutral statements about Bob in part 2 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (g) whether they noticed any change in the valence of the statements from part 1 to part 2 of the learning phase (no, positive to negative, negative to positive); (h) how they explained this change (if they noticed any; free response); (i) the relative importance of part 1 versus part 2 of the learning phase in learning about Bob's true character (part 1, part 2, same, unsure); and their agreement with the statements that (j) good people can become bad and (k) bad people can become good (using 101-point sliding scales).

Participants were asked to indicate (a) their age (in years), (b) their gender (free response), (c) their race (Black or African American, American Indian or Alaska Native, White, Asian, Hispanic, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, and/or other), and (d)

Participants were asked to indicate (a) the percentage of positive statements about the experimental target that were true in part 1 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (b) the percentage of negative statements about the experimental target that were true in part 1 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (c) the percentage of positive statements about the experimental target that were true in part 2 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (d) the percentage of negative statements about the experimental target that were true in part 2 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (e) whether they noticed any change in the valence of the statements about the experimental target from part 1 to part 2 of the learning phase (no, positive to negative, negative to positive); (f) how they explained this change (if they noticed any; free response); (g) the relative importance of part 1 versus part 2 of the learning phase in learning about the experimental target's true character (part 1, part 2, same, unsure); and their rating of the believability of the information about the experimental target (h) presented in part 1 of the learning phase, (i) presented in part 2 of the learning phase, and (j) overall (using 101-point sliding scales).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: No matter its theoretical interpretation, the behavioral dissociation between implicit and explicit evaluation updating in Rydell et al. (2007) is a noteworthy behavioral finding in its own right. Additionally, this finding has also often been cited as evidence supporting dual-mode theories of attitude acquisition and change. However, the accuracy and explanatory power of these theories have increasingly been questioned in light of both empirical challenges to classic findings of implicit-explicit dissociations (Aust et al., in press; Moran et al., 2020) and new original results suggesting overlap in the processes via which implicit and explicit evaluations form and change (Cone & Ferguson, 2015; Kurdi et al., 2025; Mann & Ferguson, 2015; Peters & Gawronski, 2011; Van Dessel et al., 2019). In fact, the accumulation of these results has prompted some authors to shift toward single-process propositional frameworks suggesting that both implicit and explicit attitudes can be updated through flexible, rule-based reasoning (De Houwer, 2014; information, using a multi-condition parametric impression formation task based on Rydell et al. (2007). Specifically, as in Rydell et al. (2007), participants learned 100 pieces of positive information about a target, followed by 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, or 100 pieces of negative (counterattitudinal) information, depending on condition assignment. Like the original experiment, this study was conducted in the lab with a sample of U.S. undergraduates. To ensure adequate power, the sample size was increased nearly fivefold relative to the original. As noted above, the original study reported that implicit evaluations changed continuously, whereas explicit evaluations changed asymptotically in response to increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 133 columns across 7 data files.
#### Issues Identified

3 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("[Anonymized] (202X) Exp. 1.csv", "[Anonymized] (202X) Exp. 2.csv", "[Anonymized] (202X) Supplementary Experiment.csv"), Column = c("exp_check8", "exp_check6", "exp_check8"), Issues = c("🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: no change/No change
🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 104 characters, 99% distinct, 36% written ...", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 95 characters, 100% distinct, 33% written ...", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: no change/No change
🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 102 characters, 99% distinct, 39% written ..." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 7 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: In the Rydell et al. (2007) paradigm, participants were introduced to a novel target named Bob and learned about him via an impression formation procedure relying on valenced behavioral statements.
A total of 598 participants were recruited from the study pools at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Yale University, and Williams College.

Participants were excluded from analyses if they (a) did not complete the Implicit Association Test (IAT), which served as the key dependent measure (n = 2), or (b) had response latencies below 300 ms on 10% or more of IAT trials, indicating inattention (Greenwald et al., 2003; n = 1).

Participants were randomly assigned to one of six between-participant conditions, which determined the number of counterattitudinal (CA) statements to which they were exposed in the second part of the learning phase: (a) 0 CA (n = 101), (b) 20 CA (n = 96), (c) 40 CA (n = 101), (d) 60 CA (n = 108), (e) 80 CA (n = 102), and (f) 100 CA (n = 87).
Finally, participants completed some exploratory items and some basic demographic items.
On the first 100 trials, participants were exposed to 50 positive and 50 negative behavioral statements.

In the 0 CA condition, which served as a control condition, participants were exposed to 100 neutral behavioral statements, half of which were randomly assigned to be characteristic and half uncharacteristic of Bob.

In the remaining conditions, participants were first exposed to a number of CA statements (in one block), followed by a number of neutral statements to ensure that all participants completed the same number of trials.
For example, in the 60 CA condition, participants were first exposed to 30 uncharacteristic positive and 30 characteristic negative statements, followed by 40 neutral statements.
Finally, in block 5 (second critical block; 20 trials), participants completed a combined sorting task opposite of the one they had completed in block 3.
A total of 499 participants were recruited from the study pools at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Yale University, and Williams College.
Participants were excluded from analyses if they (a) did not complete the IAT (n = 3) or (b) had response latencies below 300 ms on 10% or more of IAT trials (n = 1).

Participants were randomly assigned to one of seven between-participant conditions, which determined the amount of counterattitudinal information to which they were exposed in the second part of the learning phase: (a) control (n = 73), (b) 20 CA (n = 68), (c) 40 CA (n = 67), (d) 60 CA (n = 77), (e) 80 CA (n = 68), (f) 100 CA (n = 71), and (g) 1 CA (n = 71).
To ensure appropriate retention of the newly presented information, participants were required to read each statement for at least 30 seconds before they were able to proceed to the next screen.

In the 20 CA, 40 CA, 60 CA, 80 CA, and 100 CA conditions, participants were exposed to a number of counterattitudinal behavioral statements following the same trial structure as part 1 of the learning phase.

For example, in the 60 CA condition, participants were exposed to 30 uncharacteristic positive and 30 characteristic negative statements about the experimental target, along with 12 characteristic neutral statements about the control target.
Participants completed the explicit evaluation items both for the control target (Cronbach's α = .98) and the experimental target (Cronbach's α = .93), in randomized order.

Participants were asked to indicate (a) the percentage of positive statements about Bob that were true in part 1 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (b) the percentage of negative statements about Bob that were true in part 1 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (c) the percentage of neutral statements about Bob in part 1 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (d) the percentage of positive statements about Bob that were true in part 2 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (e) the percentage of negative statements about Bob that were true in part 2 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (f) the percentage of neutral statements about Bob in part 2 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (g) whether they noticed any change in the valence of the statements from part 1 to part 2 of the learning phase (no, positive to negative, negative to positive); (h) how they explained this change (if they noticed any; free response); (i) the relative importance of part 1 versus part 2 of the learning phase in learning about Bob's true character (part 1, part 2, same, unsure); and their agreement with the statements that (j) good people can become bad and (k) bad people can become good (using 101-point sliding scales).

Participants were asked to indicate (a) their age (in years), (b) their gender (free response), (c) their race (Black or African American, American Indian or Alaska Native, White, Asian, Hispanic, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, and/or other), and (d)

Participants were asked to indicate (a) the percentage of positive statements about the experimental target that were true in part 1 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (b) the percentage of negative statements about the experimental target that were true in part 1 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (c) the percentage of positive statements about the experimental target that were true in part 2 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (d) the percentage of negative statements about the experimental target that were true in part 2 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (e) whether they noticed any change in the valence of the statements about the experimental target from part 1 to part 2 of the learning phase (no, positive to negative, negative to positive); (f) how they explained this change (if they noticed any; free response); (g) the relative importance of part 1 versus part 2 of the learning phase in learning about the experimental target's true character (part 1, part 2, same, unsure); and their rating of the believability of the information about the experimental target (h) presented in part 1 of the learning phase, (i) presented in part 2 of the learning phase, and (j) overall (using 101-point sliding scales).

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 1 R code file.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1L, File = "[Anonymized] (202X) Analysis Script.R", 
    "Runs after" = "—", Basis = "numeric"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 1 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **A script looked for 3 files in another folder than the deposit has them**, so before running it once more we copied them there: `Experiment 1/[Anonymized] (202X) Exp. 1.csv` to `[Anonymized] (202X) Exp. 1.csv` for `[Anonymized] (202X) Analysis Script.R`; `Experiment 2/[Anonymized] (202X) Exp. 2.csv` to `[Anonymized] (202X) Exp. 2.csv` for `[Anonymized] (202X) Analysis Script.R`; `Supplementary Experiment/[Anonymized] (202X) Supplementary Experiment.csv` to `[Anonymized] (202X) Supplementary Experiment.csv` for `[Anonymized] (202X) Analysis Script.R`. Building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "[Anonymized] (202X) Analysis Script.R", 
    Outcome = "ran_ok", Detail = "", "Time (s)" = 13.4), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: [Anonymized] (202X) Analysis Script.R.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "[Anonymized] (202X) Analysis Script.R", 
    "setwd() removed" = 1L, "Path(s) it set" = "(non-literal)"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Calls that install packages in the code**

8 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

text.text: documented a dissociative pattern of updating such that implicit (automatic) evaluations changed continuously, whereas explicit (controlled) evaluations changed asymptotically in response to increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information.
In the present project (total N = 1,090; preregistered), we revisited this finding to examine the functional form of evaluative updating and probe its robustness across procedural variations.
In Experiment 1, which implemented a parametric learning procedure based on the original task, implicit evaluations changed asymptotically, whereas explicit evaluations changed continuously.
In Experiment 2, which introduced modifications to the learning and test phases, both implicit and explicit evaluations changed asymptotically.
These results suggest that the functional trajectories of evaluative learning are highly variable across procedural parameters.
Because these divergent patterns are challenging to reconcile with any single existing theoretical account, they underscore the value of grounding future research in quantitative models of learning.
We define attitudes as latent evaluative knowledge linking social entities to positive and/or negative valence in long-term memory (e.g., Fazio, 2007).
text.formatted: We define attitudes as latent evaluative knowledge linking social entities to positive and/or negative valence in long-term memory (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Fazio, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: We do not make any assumptions about the format of the corresponding mental representations (e.g., associative vs. propositional).

We use the term "evaluations" to refer to observable evaluative behaviors, such as button presses on the Implicit Association Test (IAT) or selecting a scale value on a semantic differential item (Cunningham & Zelazo, 2007).
text.formatted: We use the term "evaluations" to refer to observable evaluative behaviors, such as button presses on the Implicit Association Test (IAT) or selecting a scale value on a semantic differential item <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cunningham & Zelazo, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Within evaluations, we juxtapose implicit with explicit evaluations, with the former retrieved under conditions of automaticity and the latter under more controlled conditions (De Houwer et al., 2009; Moors & De Houwer, 2006).
text.formatted: Within evaluations, we juxtapose implicit with explicit evaluations, with the former retrieved under conditions of automaticity and the latter under more controlled conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(De Houwer et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Moors & De Houwer, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: In the present work, we focus on a key but surprisingly understudied determinant of attitude change: the amount of counterattitudinal information.

A naïve account might suggest that more counterattitudinal information should create stronger change in attitudes. 2 However, several -seemingly fundamentally different -perspectives from the cognitive sciences imply that this need not be the case.
text.formatted: A naïve account might suggest that more counterattitudinal information should create stronger change in attitudes. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">2</ref> However, several -seemingly fundamentally different -perspectives from the cognitive sciences imply that this need not be the case.

text.text: For example, classic theories of associative learning, such as the Rescorla-Wagner model, posit that additional information will not have any effect unless it creates a prediction error, i.e., it is surprising from the organism's perspective (Rescorla & Wagner, 1972).
text.formatted: For example, classic theories of associative learning, such as the Rescorla-Wagner model, posit that additional information will not have any effect unless it creates a prediction error, i.e., it is surprising from the organism's perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Rescorla & Wagner, 1972)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, under Bayesian accounts, updating is continuous but subject to diminishing returns: As prior beliefs strengthen, the incremental impact of each new piece of evidence approaches zero (Tenenbaum et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Similarly, under Bayesian accounts, updating is continuous but subject to diminishing returns: As prior beliefs strengthen, the incremental impact of each new piece of evidence approaches zero <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Tenenbaum et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, even if additional counterattitudinal information produces some effect, change need not scale linearly with more pieces of evidence.
For example, the first few pieces of counterattitudinal information may be more impactful than later ones because they are more surprising.

Driven by these considerations, in this paper we revisit a classic study by Rydell et al. (2007) using a parametric design based on the original learning task (Experiment 1) alongside a modified paradigm testing robustness across procedural variations (Experiment 2) to investigate how implicit and explicit evaluations change in response to increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information.

(2007)</ref> using a parametric design based on the original learning task (Experiment 1) alongside a modified paradigm testing robustness across procedural variations (Experiment 2) to investigate how implicit and explicit evaluations change in response to increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information.

text.text: In the Rydell et al. (2007) paradigm, participants were introduced to a novel target named Bob and learned about him via an impression formation procedure relying on valenced behavioral statements.
text.formatted: In the <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref> paradigm, participants were introduced to a novel target named Bob and learned about him via an impression formation procedure relying on valenced behavioral statements.

text.text: In part 1 of the learning phase (attitude formation), all 50 positively valenced behavioral statements were revealed to be characteristic and all 50 negatively valenced behavioral statements to be uncharacteristic of Bob, which was expected to create a uniformly positive impression of him.
In part 2 of the learning phase (attitude change), 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, or 100 counterattitudinal (CA; uncharacteristic positive and characteristic negative) statements were presented.
To ensure that participants across all conditions encountered the same number of statements, neutral statements were used as fillers.
For example, in the 60 CA condition, participants encountered 40 neutral statements to bring the total number of statements up to 100.

In the test phase, relatively automatic (implicit) aspects of evaluative responding were measured using an Implicit Association Test (IAT; Greenwald et al., 1998), whereas relatively controlled (explicit) aspects of evaluative responding were measured using semantic differential items and a feeling thermometer.
text.formatted: In the test phase, relatively automatic (implicit) aspects of evaluative responding were measured using an Implicit Association Test (IAT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Greenwald et al., 1998)</ref>, whereas relatively controlled (explicit) aspects of evaluative responding were measured using semantic differential items and a feeling thermometer.

text.text: Remarkably, Rydell et al.'s (2007) data revealed fundamentally different patterns of updating in implicit versus explicit evaluations in response to increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information: Implicit evaluations changed continuously; that is, each additional statement produced an incremental effect, with no leveling off even after 100 statements.
text.formatted: Remarkably, <ref type="bibr">Rydell et al.'s (2007)</ref> data revealed fundamentally different patterns of updating in implicit versus explicit evaluations in response to increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information: Implicit evaluations changed continuously; that is, each additional statement produced an incremental effect, with no leveling off even after 100 statements.

text.text: By contrast, explicit evaluation updating asymptoted immediately, with 20 pieces of counterattitudinal information producing a quick reversal and additional statements resulting in no incremental benefit.

As such, at the behavioral level 3 , these data suggest a clear dissociation between implicit and explicit evaluations, with the former exhibiting a continuous (and even linear) and the latter an (immediately) asymptotic pattern.
We note that Rydell et al. (2007) used the terms "incremental" and "abrupt" to describe these results.
text.formatted: We note that <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref> used the terms "incremental" and "abrupt" to describe these results.

text.text: Here we do not use this terminology because intermediate patterns of change are also possible.
For example, it is conceivable for change to be relatively large between the control (0 CA) and 20 CA conditions, with the remaining conditions producing smaller, linear amounts of updating.
Updating could also asymptote past 20 CA statements, e.g., at 40 or 60 CA statements.
As such, in this paper we distinguish between asymptotic change (showing a saturation point) and continuous change (without a clear saturation point).

Within asymptotic change, we distinguish between an immediate asymptote (at 20 CA statements; see explicit evaluations in Rydell et al., 2007) versus a delayed asymptote (at 40 or more CA statements).
text.formatted: Within asymptotic change, we distinguish between an immediate asymptote (at 20 CA statements; see explicit evaluations in <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al., 2007)</ref> versus a delayed asymptote (at 40 or more CA statements).

text.text: Within continuous change, different patterns are conceivable, including linear change (where each CA statement produces roughly equivalent effects; see implicit evaluations in Rydell et al., 2007), biphasic change (an initial burst followed by shallower linear updating), and diminishing returns (with the incremental benefit of each additional statement decreasing but not reaching zero).
text.formatted: Within continuous change, different patterns are conceivable, including linear change (where each CA statement produces roughly equivalent effects; see implicit evaluations in <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al., 2007)</ref>, biphasic change (an initial burst followed by shallower linear updating), and diminishing returns (with the incremental benefit of each additional statement decreasing but not reaching zero).

text.text: At the cognitive level, Rydell et al. (2007) interpreted the observed implicit-explicit dissociation as supporting the systems of evaluation model (SEM; McConnell & Rydell, 2014; Rydell & McConnell, 2006).

(2007)</ref> interpreted the observed implicit-explicit dissociation as supporting the systems of evaluation model (SEM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">McConnell & Rydell, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Rydell & McConnell, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: This dual-mode account juxtaposes an associative and a propositional system of evaluation with each other (see also Gawronski & Bodenhausen, 2006; Smith & De-Coster, 2000; Strack & Deutsch, 2004).
text.formatted: This dual-mode account juxtaposes an associative and a propositional system of evaluation with each other (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Gawronski & Bodenhausen, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Smith & De-Coster, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Strack & Deutsch, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, the SEM assumes that implicit evaluations emerge from an associative cognitive system in which associative representations (such as BOB-GOOD) are being updated piecemeal with each incoming piece of information (hence the observed continuous pattern of change).

By contrast, according to the SEM, explicit evaluations emerge from a propositional cognitive system, which is capable of performing quick, rule-based reasoning (hence the observed asymptotic pattern of change).
Why did we deem it valuable to revisit the Rydell et al. (2007) paradigm?
text.formatted: Why did we deem it valuable to revisit the <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref> paradigm?

text.text: One key justification for conducting this work was that although amount of counterattitudinal information is arguably among the most important aspects of counterattitudinal updating, few experimental studies, and especially few empirical studies featuring both measures of implicit and explicit evaluation, have investigated its effects.

Accordingly, the Rydell et al. (2007) experiment is an important empirical contribution to the literature on attitude change and thus serves as a reasonable starting point for any investigation of the influence of increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information on evaluative responding.
text.formatted: Accordingly, the <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref> experiment is an important empirical contribution to the literature on attitude change and thus serves as a reasonable starting point for any investigation of the influence of increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information on evaluative responding.

text.text: Nevertheless, to our knowledge, no prior research has systematically revisited or built upon this parametric paradigm.
No matter its theoretical interpretation, the behavioral dissociation between implicit and explicit evaluation updating in Rydell et al. (2007) is a noteworthy behavioral finding in its own right.
text.formatted: No matter its theoretical interpretation, the behavioral dissociation between implicit and explicit evaluation updating in <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref> is a noteworthy behavioral finding in its own right.

text.text: Additionally, this finding has also often been cited as evidence supporting dual-mode theories of attitude acquisition and change.

However, the accuracy and explanatory power of these theories have increasingly been questioned in light of both empirical challenges to classic findings of implicit-explicit dissociations (Aust et al., in press; Moran et al., 2020) and new original results suggesting overlap in the processes via which implicit and explicit evaluations form and change (Cone & Ferguson, 2015; Kurdi et al., 2025; Mann & Ferguson, 2015; Peters & Gawronski, 2011; Van Dessel et al., 2019).

text.text: Like the original experiment, this study was conducted in the lab with a sample of U.S. undergraduates.
To ensure adequate power, the sample size was increased nearly fivefold relative to the original.

As noted above, the original study reported that implicit evaluations changed continuously, whereas explicit evaluations changed asymptotically in response to increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information.
A total of 598 participants were recruited from the study pools at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Yale University, and Williams College.
The experiment was conducted in the lab at each of the three data collection sites.
Participants received partial course credit.

Participants were excluded from analyses if they (a) did not complete the Implicit Association Test (IAT), which served as the key dependent measure (n = 2), or (b) had response latencies below 300 ms on 10% or more of IAT trials, indicating inattention (Greenwald et al., 2003; n = 1).

text.text: These exclusions resulted in a final sample size of 595 (n = 489 at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, n = 74 at Williams College, and n = 32 at Yale University).

text.text: Mean age was 19 years (SD = 1). 221 participants identified as White, 142 participants as Asian, 68 participants as Hispanic, 57 participants as multiracial, 40 participants as Black or African American, 7 participants as other, and 60 participants did not report. 285 participants grew up speaking only English at home, 171 participants English and another language, 81 participants only a language other than English, and 58 participants did not report.
Because none of these variables moderated any of the key results, they are not discussed further.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of six between-participant conditions, which determined the number of counterattitudinal (CA) statements to which they were exposed in the second part of the learning phase: (a) 0 CA (n = 101), (b) 20 CA (n = 96), (c) 40 CA (n = 101), (d) 60 CA (n = 108), (e) 80 CA (n = 102), and (f) 100 CA (n = 87).
Part 1 of the learning phase, in which baseline evaluations were induced, and the test phase, consisting of measurement of implicit and explicit evaluations, were identical across conditions.

text.text: Behavioral Statements. 50 positive and 50 negative behavioral statements were selected for use in part 1 of the learning phase; 50 positive, 50 negative, and 100 neutral behavioral statements were selected for use in part 2 of the learning phase.
Facial Images.
Six facial images of White men were used.
One of these images was randomly assigned to serve as Bob, whereas the remaining images served as control images on the implicit evaluation measure.

The experiment consisted of (a) a learning phase during which participants learned about a novel target called Bob and (b) a test phase in which implicit and explicit evaluations of Bob were measured in randomized order.
Finally, participants completed some exploratory items and some basic demographic items.
Learning Phase.
The learning phase consisted of an impression formation task.
On each trial, the image of Bob was presented in the center of the screen, with a behavioral statement (e.g., "Bob paid a man to follow his wife around") displayed below.
Participants' task was to use their keyboard to indicate whether the statement was characteristic (C key) or uncharacteristic (U key) of Bob.
Reminders of the two response keys were displayed in the top left and right corners of the screen throughout.
When participants entered a response, the image of Bob and the behavioral statement were removed from the screen.

If the response was accurate, the word "CORRECT" printed in green letters was displayed for 1,000 ms; if the response was inaccurate, the word "FALSE" printed in red letters was displayed for 1,000 ms.
The impression formation task consisted of 200 trials.
On the first 100 trials, participants were exposed to 50 positive and 50 negative behavioral statements.
All positive behavioral statements were revealed to be characteristic and all negative behavioral statements to be uncharacteristic of Bob.
The purpose of these trials was to induce positive evaluations of Bob.
The second set of 100 trials was determined by participants' condition assignment.

In the 0 CA condition, which served as a control condition, participants were exposed to 100 neutral behavioral statements, half of which were randomly assigned to be characteristic and half uncharacteristic of Bob.

In the remaining conditions, participants were first exposed to a number of CA statements (in one block), followed by a number of neutral statements to ensure that all participants completed the same number of trials.
For example, in the 60 CA condition, participants were first exposed to 30 uncharacteristic positive and 30 characteristic negative statements, followed by 40 neutral statements.
The positive and negative statements were selected from a set of 50 statements each and presented in randomly intermixed order.
The 100 CA condition featured all positive and negative statements and no neutral statements.
Test Phase.
In the test phase, implicit and explicit evaluations of Bob were measured in randomized order, followed by a set of exploratory measures and some demographic items.
Implicit evaluations of Bob were measured using a version of the 5-block Implicit Association Test (IAT; Greenwald et al., 1998).
text.formatted: Implicit evaluations of Bob were measured using a version of the 5-block Implicit Association Test (IAT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Greenwald et al., 1998)</ref>.

text.text: In block 1 (category practice; 10 trials), participants practiced sorting the six facial images of White men into the categories "Bob" and "Not Bob."
In block 2 (attribute practice; 10 trials), participants practiced sorting attribute words into the attributes "Positive" and "Negative."

In block 3 (first critical block; 20 trials), the two categorization tasks were combined such that participants sorted Bob images and positive attribute words using one response key and not-Bob images and negative attribute words using the other response key or vice versa (depending on random assignment).
In block 4 (reverse category practice; 10 trials), participants practiced sorting the new assignment of the "Bob" and "Not Bob" categories to response keys.
Finally, in block 5 (second critical block; 20 trials), participants completed a combined sorting task opposite of the one they had completed in block 3.
For example, if in block 3 Bob images and positive attribute words were assigned to the same response key, in block 5 Bob images and negative attribute words were assigned to the same response key.
Participants used the E and I keys on their keyboards to respond.
If they responded incorrectly, a red X was displayed until participants corrected their response after which they were allowed to proceed to the next trial.
The D1 algorithm (Greenwald et al., 2003) was used to derive IAT D scores.
text.formatted: The D1 algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Greenwald et al., 2003)</ref> was used to derive IAT D scores.

text.text: IAT D scores were calculated such that higher scores indicate more positive evaluations of Bob (and/or more negative evaluations of the control targets).
Explicit evaluations of Bob were measured using a seven-item scale, with the items presented in the same fixed order to all participants.

The first six items were 9-point semantic differential scales with the endpoints labeled "very unlikable"-"very likable", "bad"-"good", "mean"-"pleasant", "disagreeable"-"agreeable", "uncaring"-"caring", and "cruel"-"kind," respectively.

Finally, participants used a 101-point sliding scale to rate their feelings toward Bob, ranging from 0° (extremely unfavorable) to 100° (extremely favorable), with the midpoint marked 50° (neither favorable nor unfavorable).
After recoding the feeling thermometer item to a 9-point scale, the seven items (Cronbach's α = .97) were averaged to form an overall evaluative index.

To parallel IAT D scores, 5 was subtracted from the composite scores to ensure that 0 represented neutrality. the language they spoke at home growing up (only English, English and some other language, only a language other than English, and not sure).

text.text: As preregistered, two sets of analyses were conducted.
Implicit and explicit evaluations were standardized to standard deviation units for both sets of analyses.
No centering was performed to ensure that zero corresponded to neutrality (rather than the sample mean).
To allow for direct comparability, the first set of analyses replicated the analytic strategy followed by Rydell et al. (2007).
text.formatted: To allow for direct comparability, the first set of analyses replicated the analytic strategy followed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, we used the rstatix package (version 0.7.3; Kassambara, 2025) to fit a mixed-design analysis of variance (ANOVA) to the data, with experimental condition (0 CA, 20 CA, 40 CA, 60 CA, 80 CA, or 100 CA) as a between-participant factor and evaluation type (implicit vs. explicit) as a within-participant factor.
As preregistered, the significant interaction was followed up by separate one-way ANOVAs fit to the implicit and explicit evaluation data, respectively.
Condition differences were determined using Tukey's Honest Significant Difference (HSD) method.
The second set of analyses were conducted via mixed-effects modeling using the lme4 package (version 1.1-23; Bates et al., 2015).
text.formatted: The second set of analyses were conducted via mixed-effects modeling using the lme4 package (version 1.1-23; <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bates et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The random part of the model included random intercepts for participants and data collection sites.

For the fixed part of the model, we relied on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) to identify the best-fitting model among five candidates, including (a) a null (intercept-only) model, (b) a model including only a main effect of experimental condition, (c) a model including only a main effect of evaluation type, (d) a model including both main effects, and (e) a model including both main effects and the interaction.
Confidence intervals were calculated and follow-up comparisons conducted using the emmeans package (version 1.5.0; Lenth et al., 2023), with the Tukey method used to adjust for multiple comparisons.
text.formatted: Confidence intervals were calculated and follow-up comparisons conducted using the emmeans package (version 1.5.0; <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Lenth et al., 2023)</ref>, with the Tukey method used to adjust for multiple comparisons.

text.text: We report linear mixed-effects modeling analyses alongside the ANOVA framework used by Rydell et al. (2007) to account for the multi-site nature of data collection.
text.formatted: We report linear mixed-effects modeling analyses alongside the ANOVA framework used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref> to account for the multi-site nature of data collection.

text.text: This approach allows for the simultaneous modeling of random intercepts for individual participants and data collection sites, thus accounting for laboratory-specific variance and preserving statistical power without inflating Type I error rates.
Fitting both types of models also served as a check on the robustness of the statistical inferences.
To examine updating trajectories within an established paradigm, Experiment 1 implemented the design, stimulus materials, and key dependent measures of Rydell et al. (2007) without modification.
text.formatted: To examine updating trajectories within an established paradigm, Experiment 1 implemented the design, stimulus materials, and key dependent measures of <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref> without modification.

text.text: Specifically, the behavioral statements, target and control photographs, the learning schedule (100 positive trials followed by 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, or 100 negative trials), as well as the test phase (including the IAT and self-report measures) were identical across the two experiments.
Four procedural features differed between Rydell et al. (2007) and the present experiment.
text.formatted: Four procedural features differed between <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref> and the present experiment.

text.text: First, whereas Rydell et al. tested 132 undergraduates at a single institution, the present experiment tested 595 undergraduates across three sites to ensure high statistical power.
Second, following each participant response during the learning phase, feedback was displayed for 1,000 ms rather than 5,000 ms to prevent participant fatigue.
Third, the exploratory self-report items following the key dependent measures were not present in the original study.
Finally, brief demographic questions were administered at the conclusion of the experimental session.
The distribution of implicit and explicit evaluations is shown in Figure 1.

text.text: Consistent with the experimental manipulation, implicit evaluations were positive in the 0 CA condition (M = 0.60, SD = 0.47).

Reflecting the effects of counterattitudinal information, positivity was attenuated in all remaining conditions, including 20 CA (M = 0.39, SD = 0.37), 40 CA (M = 0.49, SD = 0.45), 60 CA (M = 0.40, SD = 0.43), 80 CA (M = 0.34, SD = 0.52), and 100 CA (M = 0.38, SD = 0.55).
Critically, all counterattitudinal conditions were characterized by highly similar responding.

This asymptotic pattern of updating does not align with the one reported by Rydell et al. (2007) in which implicit evaluations became continuously more negative as the number of counterattitudinal statements increased across conditions.
text.formatted: This asymptotic pattern of updating does not align with the one reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref> in which implicit evaluations became continuously more negative as the number of counterattitudinal statements increased across conditions.

text.text: Also consistent with the experimental manipulation, explicit evaluations were positive in the 0 CA condition (M = 2.29, SD = 1.40).

Reflecting the effects of counterattitudinal information, positivity was attenuated or even eliminated in all remaining conditions, including 20 CA (M = 0.24, SD = 1.26), 40 CA (M = -0.30, SD = 1.36), 60 CA (M = -0.63, SD = 1.20), 80 CA (M = -0.95, SD = 1.36), and 100 CA (M = -1.37, SD = 1.49).
Notably, the amount of updating in explicit evaluations continuously scaled with the number of counterattitudinal statements.

As such, this pattern also deviates from the asymptotic one reported by Rydell et al. (2007) in which additional counterattitudinal statements did not produce any incremental updating in explicit evaluations.
text.formatted: As such, this pattern also deviates from the asymptotic one reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref> in which additional counterattitudinal statements did not produce any incremental updating in explicit evaluations.

text.text: Accordingly, the mixed-design ANOVA yielded a significant Condition × Evaluation Type interaction, F(5, 588) = 26.71, p < .001, ηp² = .185, suggesting that the effects of increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information differed across implicit and explicit evaluations.
text.formatted: Accordingly, the mixed-design ANOVA yielded a significant Condition × Evaluation Type interaction, F(5, 588) = 26.71, p < .001, ηp² = .185, suggesting that the effects of increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information differed across implicit and explicit evaluations.

text.text: In breaking down this interaction, we found a significant condition effect on implicit evaluations, F(5, 589) = 4.02, p = .001, η² = .033.
Tukey's HSD method yielded significant differences between the 0 CA condition and each of the 20 CA, 60 CA, 80 CA, and 100 CA conditions.

None of the remaining comparisons were significant; however, the difference between the 0 CA and 40 CA conditions was in the theoretically expected direction and similar in size to the other condition differences.
We also found a significant condition effect on explicit evaluations, F(5, 588) = 92.18, p < .001, η² = .439.
