40 CA, the 40 CA vs.
60 CA, the 60 CA vs.
80 CA, and the 80 CA vs.
100 CA condition differences were not significant).

Taken together, this inferential analysis confirms the descriptive statistics reported above such that implicit evaluations shifted asymptotically (and moderately) and explicit evaluations shifted continuously (and strongly).
The mixed-effects modeling approach yielded substantially identical conclusions.
The best-fitting model included random intercepts for participants and data collection sites, as well as a significant Condition × Evaluation Type interaction, χ 2 (5) = 121.51, p < .001.
text.formatted: The best-fitting model included random intercepts for participants and data collection sites, as well as a significant Condition × Evaluation Type interaction, χ 2 (5) = 121.51, p < .001.

text.text: Identical to the ANOVA analysis, for implicit evaluations we found significant differences between the 0 CA condition and each of the 20 CA, 60 CA, 80 CA, and 100 CA conditions.
No other comparisons were significant.

Also identical to the ANOVA analysis, for explicit evaluations we obtained significant differences between the 0 CA condition and each other condition, as well as significant differences across all remaining non-adjacent conditions.
Experiment 1 investigated the functional trajectories of evaluative updating across increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information in a parametric design based on Rydell et al. (2007).
text.formatted: Experiment 1 investigated the functional trajectories of evaluative updating across increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information in a parametric design based on <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref>.

text.text: The observed trajectories revealed a distinct functional form: Implicit evaluations updated rapidly, reaching an asymptote after just 20 counterattitudinal trials, whereas explicit evaluations changed continuously across the entire range of counterattitudinal information.
These findings carry important implications for theories of evaluative learning.

Regardless of whether one adopts a dual-mode, single-process, or any other theoretical framework, any account must reckon with the finding that -at least under the parametric conditions created by the present paradigm -implicit evaluations can update asymptotically, while explicit evaluations can update incrementally.

This observed pattern stands in contrast to the results of Rydell et al. (2007) who reported the opposite dissociation: continuous updating for implicit evaluations and asymptotic updating for explicit evaluations.
text.formatted: This observed pattern stands in contrast to the results of <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref> who reported the opposite dissociation: continuous updating for implicit evaluations and asymptotic updating for explicit evaluations.

text.text: Although both studies demonstrate that implicit and explicit evaluations can diverge in their response to counterattitudinal information, they point to contradictory conclusions regarding the functional forms that govern each mode of evaluation.
We return to potential procedural and theoretical explanations for this empirical discrepancy in the General Discussion.

Experiment 1 investigated evaluative updating within the baseline paradigm of Rydell et al. (2007), observing rapid, asymptotic change for implicit evaluations alongside continuous change for explicit evaluations.
text.formatted: Experiment 1 investigated evaluative updating within the baseline paradigm of <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref>, observing rapid, asymptotic change for implicit evaluations alongside continuous change for explicit evaluations.

text.text: To determine whether these functional trajectories reflect general properties of evaluative learning or depend on specific operational parameters of the learning task, Experiment 2 introduced procedural variations to both the learning and measurement phases.
With respect to measurement, the IAT used in Experiment 1 was subject to several methodological limitations (see, e.g., Greenwald et al., 2022).
text.formatted: With respect to measurement, the IAT used in Experiment 1 was subject to several methodological limitations (see, e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Greenwald et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: First, it included only 20 trials per combined block, which is considerably below the currently recommended standard.
Second, the IAT presented the target using a single photograph against a non-specific contrast category ("Not Bob").

Third, structural correspondence between the IAT and self-report measures was limited: Whereas the former was relative (comparing Bob to a contrast category), the latter was absolute (evaluating Bob in isolation).

To address these limitations, Experiment 2 doubled the number of critical trials to 40 per block, represented both the experimental target and a specific control target using multiple unique facial photographs each, and measured evaluations of the experimental target relative to the control target on both the IAT and self-report.
With respect to the learning phase, we made several changes to address methodological and practical limitations of the baseline paradigm.
First, to introduce the control target used on the subsequent evaluation tasks, the learning phase included both the experimental and the control target.
The control target was paired with neutral behavioral statements.
In addition, unlike in Experiment 1, all neutral statements were revealed to be true of the control target, ensuring a predictable learning experience.
Second, we removed the neutral statements about the experimental target from part 2 of the learning phase.

Although keeping the total number of statements constant across participants (as in Rydell et al., 2007) equates task length, including presumably neutral statements (e.g., "Bob is from a mid-sized city") introduces two complexities: They could dilute learning effects by normalizing the target or serving as a mildly positive learning signal, and completing up to 100 trials where statements are unpredictably revealed to be true or false could create a frustrating participant experience.
text.formatted: Although keeping the total number of statements constant across participants (as in <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al., 2007)</ref> equates task length, including presumably neutral statements (e.g., "Bob is from a mid-sized city") introduces two complexities: They could dilute learning effects by normalizing the target or serving as a mildly positive learning signal, and completing up to 100 trials where statements are unpredictably revealed to be true or false could create a frustrating participant experience.

text.text: Therefore, in the counterattitudinal conditions of Experiment 2, part 2 included only valenced statements about the experimental target, along with a smaller number of neutral statements about the control target.
Finally, parts 1 and 2 of the learning phase were clearly separated by instructions.

In addition, results by Ferguson and colleagues (e.g., Cone & Ferguson, 2015; Kurdi et al., 2026; Mann & Ferguson, 2015; Surdel & Ferguson, 2026), produced over the past ten years, suggest that, under certain conditions, implicit (and explicit) evaluations can shift rapidly and substantially in response to a single piece of information (for a review, see Ferguson et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In addition, results by <ref type="bibr">Ferguson and colleagues (e.g., Cone & Ferguson, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Kurdi et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Mann & Ferguson, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Surdel & Ferguson, 2026)</ref>, produced over the past ten years, suggest that, under certain conditions, implicit (and explicit) evaluations can shift rapidly and substantially in response to a single piece of information (for a review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Ferguson et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Critically, this research has found that for such change to occur, information must be extreme in valence and highly diagnostic of the target's character.

Accordingly, to establish another benchmark for the power of 100 mildly valenced counterattitudinal statements in overturning initially acquired implicit (and explicit) evaluations of a social target, we also added a 1 CA condition to the learning phase of Experiment 2.

In this condition, participants learned a single piece of extremely negative and highly diagnostic information about the experimental target (specifically, that he had been convicted of child molestation; Cone & Ferguson, 2015).
text.formatted: In this condition, participants learned a single piece of extremely negative and highly diagnostic information about the experimental target (specifically, that he had been convicted of child molestation; <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Cone & Ferguson, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Because all changes described above were made simultaneously, we cannot infer with certainty which element(s) of the new experimental procedure are responsible for any potential differences in results across Experiments 1 and 2.

Rather, the aim of Experiment 2 was to (a) heuristically probe the robustness of the results of Experiment 1 and (b) adopt a design that addressed the methodological limitations of the baseline task and ensured a more predictable participant experience on control trials.
The design, materials, procedure, and measures were similar to Experiment 1, with all modifications noted below.
A total of 499 participants were recruited from the study pools at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Yale University, and Williams College.
The experiment was conducted in the lab at each of the three data collection sites.
Participants received partial course credit for their participation.
Participants were excluded from analyses if they (a) did not complete the IAT (n = 3) or (b) had response latencies below 300 ms on 10% or more of IAT trials (n = 1).

These exclusions resulted in a final sample size of 495 (n = 339 at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, n = 95 at Williams College, and n = 61 at Yale University). 358 participants identified as female, 130 as male, 4 as non-binary, and 3 did not report.

Mean age was 19 years (SD = 1). 198 participants identified as White, 135 participants as Asian, 58 participants as Hispanic, 52 participants as multiracial, 42 participants as Black or African American, 6 participants as other, and 4 participants did not report. 251 participants grew up speaking only English at home, 173 participants English and another language, 69 participants only a language other than English, and 2 participants did not report.
Because none of these variables moderated any of the key results, they are not discussed further.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of seven between-participant conditions, which determined the amount of counterattitudinal information to which they were exposed in the second part of the learning phase: (a) control (n = 73), (b) 20 CA (n = 68), (c) 40 CA (n = 67), (d) 60 CA (n = 77), (e) 80 CA (n = 68), (f) 100 CA (n = 71), and (g) 1 CA (n = 71).

In this experiment, we refer to condition (a) as the control condition rather than the 0 CA condition because, as explained above, part 2 of the learning phase did not present any neutral statements about the experimental target; as such, the control condition ended with part 1 of the learning phase.

As in Experiment 1, part 1 of the learning phase, in which baseline evaluations were induced, and the test phase, consisting of measurement of implicit and explicit evaluations, were identical across conditions.
Facial Images.
To create a more robust IAT procedure (Greenwald et al., 2022), we required facial images showing the same targets in multiple versions.
text.formatted: To create a more robust IAT procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Greenwald et al., 2022)</ref>, we required facial images showing the same targets in multiple versions.

text.text: To this end, we used four White men from the Radboud Faces Database (Langner et al., 2010), each presented in four orientations (frontal, 45° neutral, 45° left, and 45° right).
text.formatted: To this end, we used four White men from the Radboud Faces Database <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Langner et al., 2010)</ref>, each presented in four orientations (frontal, 45° neutral, 45° left, and 45° right).

text.text: One of the four individuals was randomly assigned to serve as the experimental target and another individual as the control target.
Names.
We randomly assigned a name to each target from the set "James," "Michael," "Robert," "David," "William," "Thomas," "Christopher," "Anthony," "Steven," and "Paul."
Learning Phase.
As in Experiment 1, the learning phase consisted of an impression formation task.

The initial instructions introducing this task were similar to those used in Experiment 1; however, with the exception of the control condition, they introduced the learning task as consisting of two parts.
The structure of the impression formation task trials was the same as in Experiment 1.
Part 1 of the impression formation task consisted of 120 trials. 100 trials involved the experimental target and were identical to the trials from Experiment 1.
That is, all 50 positive behavioral statements were revealed to be characteristic and all 50 negative behavioral statements were revealed to be uncharacteristic of the experimental target.
The remaining 20 behavioral statements were neutral in valence and involved the control target.
To achieve a higher level of predictability in participants' experience, all statements about the control target were revealed to be characteristic.
Statements about the experimental and control targets were presented in randomly intermixed order.
Part 2 of the learning phase was determined by participants' condition assignment.
In the control condition, the learning phase ended with the conclusion of part 1.

In the newly added 1 CA condition, participants learned that the experimental target "was recently convicted of molesting children" (Cone & Ferguson, 2015) and the control target "recently bought a soda."
text.formatted: In the newly added 1 CA condition, participants learned that the experimental target "was recently convicted of molesting children" <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cone & Ferguson, 2015)</ref> and the control target "recently bought a soda."

text.text: These two statements were presented in random order.
To ensure appropriate retention of the newly presented information, participants were required to read each statement for at least 30 seconds before they were able to proceed to the next screen.

In the 20 CA, 40 CA, 60 CA, 80 CA, and 100 CA conditions, participants were exposed to a number of counterattitudinal behavioral statements following the same trial structure as part 1 of the learning phase.
The number of statements was determined by participants' condition assignment.

For example, in the 60 CA condition, participants were exposed to 30 uncharacteristic positive and 30 characteristic negative statements about the experimental target, along with 12 characteristic neutral statements about the control target.
The number of statements about the control target was always set to 20% of the number of statements about the experimental target.
As in part 1 of the learning phase, statements about the experimental and control targets were presented in randomly intermixed order.
Test Phase.

In the test phase, implicit and explicit evaluations of the experimental target relative to the control target were measured in randomized order, followed by a set of exploratory measures and some demographic items.
The IAT procedure was modified relative to Experiment 1 in several ways.
First, the number of trials was increased from 10 to 20 for blocks 1 and 2; from 20 to 40 for block 3; from 10 to 30 in block 4; and from 20 to 40 in block 5.
Second, the names of the experimental and control targets served as category labels throughout the IAT, with each represented by four unique facial images.
Third, "Good" and "Bad" served as attribute labels and six attribute stimuli each were randomly selected from a larger set of 32 for each participant (Axt et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Third, "Good" and "Bad" served as attribute labels and six attribute stimuli each were randomly selected from a larger set of 32 for each participant <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Axt et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Participants completed the explicit evaluation items both for the control target (Cronbach's α = .98) and the experimental target (Cronbach's α = .93), in randomized order.
Mean evaluations of the control target were subtracted from mean evaluations of the experimental target, to parallel the IAT D score.
As preregistered, we used only the mixed-effects modeling approach (and not the ANOVA approach from Experiment 1) to model data from Experiment 2.
The distribution of implicit and explicit evaluations is shown in Figure 2.
text.formatted: The distribution of implicit and explicit evaluations is shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with the experimental manipulation, implicit evaluations were positive in the control condition (M = 0.29, SD = 0.49).

Reflecting the effects of counterattitudinal information, implicit evaluations were close to or at neutrality in all remaining conditions, including 20 CA (M = 0.08, SD = 0.34), 40 CA (M = 0.09, SD = 0.41), 60 CA (M = 0.03, SD = 0.39), 80 CA (M = 0.02, SD = 0.45), 100 CA (M = 0.01, SD = 0.34), and 1 CA (M = 0.00, SD = 0.41).
Similar to Experiment 1, the effects of counterattitudinal information were highly consistent across conditions, thus revealing an asymptotic pattern.
Remarkably, in the newly added 1 CA condition, a single extreme and diagnostic negative statement produced an effect indistinguishable from that achieved via 100 mildly negative statements.
Also consistent with the experimental manipulation, explicit evaluations were positive in the control condition (M = 2.33, SD = 2.27).

Reflecting the effects of counterattitudinal information, explicit evaluations were negative in all remaining conditions, including 20 CA (M = -0.79, SD = 2.44), 40 CA (M = -2.38, SD = 2.18), 60 CA (M = -2.00, SD = 2.14), 80 CA (M = -2.45, SD = 1.98), 100 CA (M = -2.11, SD = 2.35), and 1 CA (M = -2.01, SD = 2.64).
As such, unlike in Experiment 1, where explicit evaluations scaled continuously with increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information, here the incremental benefit asymptoted after 40 statements.
Similar to implicit evaluations, the effect of a single extreme and diagnostic statement was equivalent to the effect of 100 mildly valenced behavioral statements.

Accordingly, the best-fitting mixed-effects model included random intercepts for participants and data collection sites, as well as a significant Condition × Evaluation Type interaction, χ 2 (6) = 54.86, p < .001.
text.formatted: Accordingly, the best-fitting mixed-effects model included random intercepts for participants and data collection sites, as well as a significant Condition × Evaluation Type interaction, χ 2 (6) = 54.86, p < .001.

text.text: For implicit evaluations we found significant differences between the control condition and each other condition, with no other significant comparisons.
This result suggests that, similar to Experiment 1, implicit evaluations changed asymptotically rather than continuously.

For explicit evaluations, the control condition was significantly different from each other condition; moreover, the 40 CA, 80 CA, and 100 CA conditions produced significantly more change than the 20 CA condition, suggesting some incremental benefit of additional statements up until but not beyond 40.
As such, unlike in Experiment 1, explicit evaluations changed asymptotically rather than continuously.

In Experiment 2, we implemented several procedural modifications to probe the generalizability of the results of Experiment 1, in which implicit evaluations changed asymptotically, whereas explicit evaluations changed continuously as a result of increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information.

The results involving implicit evaluations were consistent such that they changed asymptotically again, with an immediate asymptote at 20 counterattitudinal statements; unlike in Experiment 1, explicit evaluation change was also asymptotic, with the asymptote at 40, rather than 20, counterattitudinal statements.
In the General Discussion we speculate about the likely reasons for the discrepancy between Experiments 1 and 2.

Regardless of the specific mechanism, these results suggest that evaluative updating trajectories depend substantially on ostensibly incidental task parameters, highlighting the need for further systematic research.

Additionally, we found that a single extreme and highly diagnostic statement about the experimental target having been convicted of child molestation produced statistically equivalent amounts of both implicit and explicit evaluation change to 100 relatively mild behavioral statements, thus challenging the idea that number of statements, in and of itself, is the key determinant of updating.
Moreover, similar to Experiment 1, we observed stronger effects of counterattitudinal information on explicit than on implicit evaluations overall.
We revisit both of these findings -which are not at the core of the present project but are nonetheless of theoretical and practical interest -in more detail in the General Discussion.
In Rydell et al. (2007), implicit evaluations updated continuously and linearly, whereas explicit evaluations changed abruptly, reaching an immediate asymptote at 20 counterattitudinal statements.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref>, implicit evaluations updated continuously and linearly, whereas explicit evaluations changed abruptly, reaching an immediate asymptote at 20 counterattitudinal statements.

text.text: In Experiment 1, we observed a pattern that diverged substantially from these functional forms: Implicit evaluation updating asymptoted at 20 statements, whereas explicit evaluations tracked continuously across the full range of counterattitudinal information.
A key question concerns why the updating trajectories differed across the two investigations.
Experiment 1 was characterized by four procedural differences relative to Rydell et al. (2007).
text.formatted: Experiment 1 was characterized by four procedural differences relative to <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref>.

text.text: Three of these can be readily ruled out as having had any plausible impact on the patterns of updating observed: (a) collecting data across three university laboratories rather than a single site (a difference explicitly accounted for via random intercepts in all mixed-effects models), (b) administering exploratory items assessing contingency awareness and attributions of change, and (c) collecting basic demographic information.
Crucially, both the exploratory and demographic items were administered at the end of the experimental session; as such, they could not have influenced responding on the main dependent measures.
The fourth procedural departure was the display duration of the post-response feedback ("CORRECT" vs.
"FALSE") during the learning phase, which was presented for 1,000 ms in the present work compared to 5,000 ms in Rydell et al. (2007) to reduce participant fatigue.
text.formatted: "FALSE") during the learning phase, which was presented for 1,000 ms in the present work compared to 5,000 ms in <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref> to reduce participant fatigue.

text.text: Notably, work on category learning suggests that feedback timing can impact information processing.

For instance, manipulating feedback duration during perceptual categorization has been shown to alter the speed of classification learning (Dolguikh et al., 2021), and delaying the onset of feedback can impair information integration (Maddox et al., 2003).
text.formatted: For instance, manipulating feedback duration during perceptual categorization has been shown to alter the speed of classification learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Dolguikh et al., 2021)</ref>, and delaying the onset of feedback can impair information integration <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Maddox et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, work on attitude formation indicates that cognitive load and time constraints can hinder the processing of negated behavioral information, potentially biasing initial evaluative encoding (Boucher & Rydell, 2012).
text.formatted: In addition, work on attitude formation indicates that cognitive load and time constraints can hinder the processing of negated behavioral information, potentially biasing initial evaluative encoding <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Boucher & Rydell, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, one could surmise that the 5,000 ms feedback window in the original study afforded additional opportunity for reflective processing or memory encoding that was constrained by the 1,000 ms window used in the present experiments.
However, upon closer inspection, we believe that feedback display duration is unlikely to account for the divergence in trajectories observed across studies.

First, participants in both of the present experiments exhibited high trial-level accuracy during the learning task (91.3% in Experiment 1 and 93.0% in Experiment 2), demonstrating that 1,000 ms of feedback was sufficient to detect and learn both the initial and reversed contingencies.
Second, reading the behavioral statement and entering a response were self-paced in both studies; only the feedback display was timed.

Third, even if reduced feedback duration had diminished the depth of processing, such a constraint should have produced a quantitative decrement in the overall slope or magnitude of updating, rather than a qualitative change in functional forms.
A second substantive consideration concerns the stimulus materials.

In the nearly two decades elapsed since Rydell et al. (2007) conducted their experiment, the normative valence, extremity, or perceived diagnosticity of the 100 behavioral statements may have shifted within undergraduate populations.
text.formatted: In the nearly two decades elapsed since <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref> conducted their experiment, the normative valence, extremity, or perceived diagnosticity of the 100 behavioral statements may have shifted within undergraduate populations.

text.text: Because neither the original study nor the present project involved empirical pretesting to norm individual items, subtle differences in how contemporary participants interpreted the evaluative information presented to them as part of the learning task cannot be ruled out.

Nonetheless, as with the feedback duration account, shifts in stimulus extremity or diagnosticity seem to provide an incomplete explanation for the divergent trajectories: Such shifts would be expected to influence the overall magnitude or slope of evaluative change, rather than qualitatively transform the functional form of updating.

Indeed, as demonstrated in Experiment 2, even introducing an extreme and diagnostic behavioral statement did not overturn the fundamental finding that implicit evaluation change can asymptote rapidly.
Taken together, the present findings carry clear theoretical implications.

Rather than reflecting an immutable, fixed cognitive architecture -in which implicit and explicit evaluations inherently operate via rigid, dissociable learning rules -these discrepancies demonstrate that the functional trajectories of evaluative updating are highly sensitive to procedural parameters, task environments, and context.

Presenting either the original dissociation or the one obtained here as a universal property of mental systems obscures the degree to which empirical updating functions are contingent on ostensibly incidental methodological choices, underscoring the need for systematic research that manipulates a wide range of learning parameters -including postresponse feedback display windows (e.g., 1,000 ms vs. 5,000 ms) -within the same paradigm.

In Experiment 2, we implemented a number of procedural improvements to the measurement of implicit evaluations; moreover, we also updated the learning phase to (a) include a specific control target and (b) omit a large number of purportedly neutral statements used as fillers in Experiment 1, which could have diluted the effects of counterattitudinal information.

Yet, despite these procedural changes, the asymptotic effect on implicit evaluations remained consistent with that observed in Experiment 1 such that 20 counterattitudinal statements were sufficient to produce updating, with no incremental effect of further information.

However, the pattern of explicit evaluations was markedly different from Experiment 1 such that in this experiment, learning also asymptoted, albeit at 40 rather than 20 counterattitudinal statements.
As such, in Experiment 2, both implicit and explicit evaluations exhibited asymptotic patterns of change.

An initial hint as to why Experiments 1 and 2 may have produced different results for explicit evaluations is provided by a supplementary experiment reported in online materials (https://osf.io/5an6x/overview?view_only=433de6a5ab954e5aa4853fb278d54b4d).
text.formatted: An initial hint as to why Experiments 1 and 2 may have produced different results for explicit evaluations is provided by a supplementary experiment reported in online materials (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/5an6x/overview?view_only=433de6a5ab954e5aa4853fb278d54b4d">https://osf.io/5an6x/overview?view_only=433de6a5ab954e5aa4853fb278d54b4d</ref>).

text.text: This round of data collection was otherwise identical to Experiment 1 but, due to a technical oversight, presented the same number of counterattitudinal and neutral statements in part 2 of the learning phase.
(For example, in the 80 CA condition, 80 counterattitudinal and 80 neutral statements were presented instead of 80 counterattitudinal and 20 neutral statements, as originally intended.)
In this experiment, similar to Experiment 2, both implicit and explicit evaluation change were asymptotic rather than continuous.

At a first approximation, this finding seems to suggest that the continuous pattern of explicit evaluations observed in Experiment 1 may have been an anomaly; moreover, it lends credence to the idea that implicit evaluations can shift asymptotically under a relatively wide range of conditions.
Although the behavioral findings of the project are unequivocal, they allow for multiple interpretations with respect to the underlying cognitive processes.

At first glance, the present results seem difficult to reconcile with the dual-systems idea originally motivating the Rydell et al. (2007) experiment, according to which implicit evaluations should change continuously and explicit evaluations should change asymptotically.
text.formatted: At first glance, the present results seem difficult to reconcile with the dual-systems idea originally motivating the <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref> experiment, according to which implicit evaluations should change continuously and explicit evaluations should change asymptotically.

text.text: Indeed, the finding that implicit evaluations, like their explicit counterparts, can change asymptotically is more seamlessly reconciled with single-process propositional accounts than with dual-mode alternatives.

To bolster this conclusion, in Experiment 2 we also found rapid, flexible updating of implicit evaluations in response to a single piece of extreme and highly diagnostic information, thus replicating and extending relevant past work (Cone & Ferguson, 2015).
text.formatted: To bolster this conclusion, in Experiment 2 we also found rapid, flexible updating of implicit evaluations in response to a single piece of extreme and highly diagnostic information, thus replicating and extending relevant past work <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cone & Ferguson, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, empirically, two sets of results run counter to a straightforward, single-process interpretation of the present findings.

First, the average amount of change observed across all experimental conditions combined relative to the control condition was vastly different between implicit and explicit evaluations in both experiments.

In Experiment 1, implicit evaluations changed by an average of 0.41 standard deviation units compared with 1.62 for explicit evaluations; in Experiment 2, the corresponding values were 0.61 versus 1.60 standard deviation units.
As such, explicit evaluations were generally more amenable to change than their implicit counterparts.
Although propositional accounts can explain the asymmetrical magnitude of change post hoc, they do not predict such a pattern a priori (see also Kurdi et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Although propositional accounts can explain the asymmetrical magnitude of change post hoc, they do not predict such a pattern a priori (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Kurdi et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Second, this discrepancy affects even the 1 CA condition of Experiment 2, in which an extremely negative piece of information created strongly negative explicit evaluations but only neutrality in implicit evaluations.
Of note, the studies reported by Cone and Ferguson (2015) found a complete reversal rather than directional change in implicit evaluations in response to the same information.
text.formatted: Of note, the studies reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Cone and Ferguson (2015)</ref> found a complete reversal rather than directional change in implicit evaluations in response to the same information.

text.text: However, those studies relied exclusively on the Affect Misattribution Procedure (AMP; Payne et al., 2005) to measure implicit evaluations, whereas the present experiments used only the Implicit Association Test (IAT).
text.formatted: However, those studies relied exclusively on the Affect Misattribution Procedure (AMP; <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Payne et al., 2005)</ref> to measure implicit evaluations, whereas the present experiments used only the Implicit Association Test (IAT).

text.text: This difference in measures may explain the divergent results given that the AMP has been found to reflect learning effects more strongly than the IAT, both generally (Kurdi et al., 2022) and specifically in the context of rapid revisions in response to diagnostic evidence (Cone & Calanchini, 2020).
text.formatted: This difference in measures may explain the divergent results given that the AMP has been found to reflect learning effects more strongly than the IAT, both generally <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Kurdi et al., 2022)</ref> and specifically in the context of rapid revisions in response to diagnostic evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cone & Calanchini, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, while the asymmetry in amounts of updating poses a clear hurdle for propositional models, it need not validate traditional dual-mode assumptions either.
Even if dual-mode frameworks broadly align with the idea that explicit evaluation change should be more robust, they fail to predict that implicit evaluations would shift rapidly in the first place.
Furthermore, purely verbal dual-mode frameworks lack the specificity to make quantitative predictions about the shape of updating curves a priori (as do their propositional counterparts).
Consequently, the asymmetrical magnitude of change points to a nuance in cognitive processing that neither theory perfectly anticipates.

This lack of a priori precision highlights the core conceptual issue complicating the theoretical interpretation of the present findings: namely, that a direct mapping from associative processes to continuous change and from propositional processes to asymptotic change is not as unassailable as may have been previously assumed.

After all, even relatively simple associative accounts of learning, such as the Rescorla-Wagner model (Rescorla & Wagner, 1972), allow for asymptotic change, including a quick or even immediate asymptote in evaluative updating, as long as the new information is particularly potent and surprising.
text.formatted: After all, even relatively simple associative accounts of learning, such as the Rescorla-Wagner model <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Rescorla & Wagner, 1972)</ref>, allow for asymptotic change, including a quick or even immediate asymptote in evaluative updating, as long as the new information is particularly potent and surprising.

text.text: Conversely, propositional processes are compatible with continuous updating.

For example, under Bayesian accounts (Tenenbaum et al., 2011), if information is low in diagnosticity (as it is in the paradigm used by Rydell et al., 2007), it should produce stepwise, moderate belief revision until a ceiling of subjective certainty is reached.
text.formatted: For example, under Bayesian accounts <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Tenenbaum et al., 2011)</ref>, if information is low in diagnosticity (as it is in the paradigm used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al., 2007)</ref>, it should produce stepwise, moderate belief revision until a ceiling of subjective certainty is reached.

text.text: As such, future work in this area would benefit from moving beyond purely verbal theories and relying on formal models of learning -broadly associative, broadly propositional, or some other kind -from which empirically testable and more easily falsifiable predictions can be derived.
Importantly, a transition toward these quantitative frameworks would also enable formal modeling of currently unexplored sources of variability in participant-level responding.

For example, differences in participants' preexisting attitudes or subtle variations in the interpretation of stimulus materials could be captured as model parameters (e.g., as Bayesian priors or the Rescorla-Wagner model's stimulus salience parameter α).
Beyond the precise mapping of behavioral results onto underlying cognitive processes, several questions in this area seem ripe for future investigation.

Notably, the present work examined only positive-to-negative updating; however, impression formation and evaluative learning are often characterized by valence asymmetry effects whereby negative information can outweigh positive information in potency and importance (Rozin & Royzman, 2001; Skowronski & Carlston, 1989; see also Cone & Ferguson, 2015).
text.formatted: Notably, the present work examined only positive-to-negative updating; however, impression formation and evaluative learning are often characterized by valence asymmetry effects whereby negative information can outweigh positive information in potency and importance <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Rozin & Royzman, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Skowronski & Carlston, 1989</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Cone & Ferguson, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: As such, whether the present results would generalize to negative-to-positive updating remains an important open question.
Moreover, the present design relied solely on an impression formation paradigm using a sequence of individual, unrelated behavioral statements to study evaluative updating.

Results may or may not generalize to paradigms involving more narrative learning (e.g., listening to podcasts; Kurdi et al., 2021), stimulus pairing-based paradigms such as evaluative conditioning (Moran et al., 2022), or learning tasks requiring more active participant engagement such as reinforcement learning (Kurdi et al., 2019; Melnikoff & Kurdi, 2025) or approach-avoidance training (Van Dessel et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Results may or may not generalize to paradigms involving more narrative learning (e.g., listening to podcasts; <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kurdi et al., 2021)</ref>, stimulus pairing-based paradigms such as evaluative conditioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Moran et al., 2022)</ref>, or learning tasks requiring more active participant engagement such as reinforcement learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Kurdi et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Melnikoff & Kurdi, 2025)</ref> or approach-avoidance training <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Van Dessel et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Because Experiment 2 served as a holistic test of generalizability by introducing multiple procedural variations simultaneously, we cannot conclusively determine which new element(s) were critical in producing the observed discrepancy in explicit evaluation updating across the two experiments.

However, the observed shift suggests that the incremental versus abrupt distinction used by Rydell et al. (2007) is insufficient to capture empirical updating profiles: In Experiment 1, explicit evaluation change was continuous but nonlinear, whereas in Experiment 2, it was asymptotic but delayed compared with implicit evaluations.
text.formatted: However, the observed shift suggests that the incremental versus abrupt distinction used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rydell et al. (2007)</ref> is insufficient to capture empirical updating profiles: In Experiment 1, explicit evaluation change was continuous but nonlinear, whereas in Experiment 2, it was asymptotic but delayed compared with implicit evaluations.

text.text: To isolate whether this shift in the explicit evaluation trajectory reflects improved measurement or a fundamental change in the learning experience itself, an important priority for follow-up work is an intermediate design.

Specifically, future research should pair the unmodified Experiment 1 learning phase (including neutral fillers) with the relative self-report measures used in Experiment 2 while systematically varying the number of neutral statements.
A related methodological consideration concerns the tracking of updating curves at the group versus individual level.

Because the between-participant design implemented here captures trajectories via group averages, it risks smoothing over intraindividual variation and introducing an artifact of data aggregation such that group-level curves do not resemble those of any individual participant (Estes, 1956; Gallistel et al., 2004); as such, future work should rely on within-participant designs.
text.formatted: Because the between-participant design implemented here captures trajectories via group averages, it risks smoothing over intraindividual variation and introducing an artifact of data aggregation such that group-level curves do not resemble those of any individual participant <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Estes, 1956;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Gallistel et al., 2004)</ref>; as such, future work should rely on within-participant designs.

text.text: Moreover, future work should directly assess whether the behavioral statements used across the learning phase were equivalent in extremity and valence. Rydell et al. (2007) did not report any pertinent pretesting data, and we did not collect such data either.

(2007)</ref> did not report any pertinent pretesting data, and we did not collect such data either.

text.text: Nevertheless, the statements do intuitively seem to differ from each other along these dimensions (e.g., "Bob belittles the minority individuals he knows" vs.
"Bob called in sick for work when he was well").
Accordingly, the internal validity of future work can be improved by using carefully normed stimulus materials (e.g., Mende-Siedlecki & Havlicek, 2025).
text.formatted: Accordingly, the internal validity of future work can be improved by using carefully normed stimulus materials (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Mende-Siedlecki & Havlicek, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A final key issue relates to the precision with which distinctions between automatic (implicit) and controlled (explicit) processes can be inferred at retrieval.

Although indirect measures (such as the IAT) are often used to index implicit evaluations and direct measures (such as semantic differentials) to index explicit evaluations, a one-to-one mapping from measures to processes cannot be assumed (Conrey et al., 2005; Jacoby, 1991).
text.formatted: Although indirect measures (such as the IAT) are often used to index implicit evaluations and direct measures (such as semantic differentials) to index explicit evaluations, a one-to-one mapping from measures to processes cannot be assumed <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Conrey et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Jacoby, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, if the goal is to establish robust differences between automatic and controlled evaluative processing, future work may be strengthened by using measures high in structural alignment (Payne et al., 2008) or process dissociation methods (Hütter & Klauer, 2016).
text.formatted: Therefore, if the goal is to establish robust differences between automatic and controlled evaluative processing, future work may be strengthened by using measures high in structural alignment <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Payne et al., 2008)</ref> or process dissociation methods <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hütter & Klauer, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: To facilitate these follow-up investigations, we provide all open materials, data, and analysis scripts used in this project, which we hope will be helpful in extending the present work to well-defined mathematical models of updating -such as associative accounts (Rescorla & Wagner, 1972) and propositional accounts of Bayesian belief revision (Tenenbaum et al., 2011) -while also reflecting these additional methodological and conceptual considerations.
text.formatted: To facilitate these follow-up investigations, we provide all open materials, data, and analysis scripts used in this project, which we hope will be helpful in extending the present work to well-defined mathematical models of updating -such as associative accounts <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Rescorla & Wagner, 1972)</ref> and propositional accounts of Bayesian belief revision <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Tenenbaum et al., 2011)</ref> -while also reflecting these additional methodological and conceptual considerations.

text.text: Rather than revealing an immutable functional dissociation between implicit and explicit evaluations, the available evidence demonstrates substantial variability in updating trajectories both across independent investigations and even within the present project itself.

Across these paradigms, one finds instances in which implicit evaluations change continuously and explicit evaluations change asymptotically (Rydell et al., 2007), implicit evaluations change asymptotically and explicit evaluations change continuously (Experiment 1), or both change asymptotically (Experiment 2).
text.formatted: Across these paradigms, one finds instances in which implicit evaluations change continuously and explicit evaluations change asymptotically <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Rydell et al., 2007)</ref>, implicit evaluations change asymptotically and explicit evaluations change continuously (Experiment 1), or both change asymptotically (Experiment 2).

text.text: As such, much remains to be understood, conceptually and empirically, about how increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information affect both relatively automatic and relatively controlled evaluative responding.

We believe that future work in this area would benefit from relying on mathematical models of learning, using normed stimulus materials and structurally aligned measures of evaluation, probing negative-to-positive in addition to positiveto-negative updating, and moving beyond exclusive reliance on impression formation paradigms.

Items.

Participants were asked to indicate (a) the percentage of positive statements about Bob that were true in part 1 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (b) the percentage of negative statements about Bob that were true in part 1 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (c) the percentage of neutral statements about Bob in part 1 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (d) the percentage of positive statements about Bob that were true in part 2 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (e) the percentage of negative statements about Bob that were true in part 2 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (f) the percentage of neutral statements about Bob in part 2 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (g) whether they noticed any change in the valence of the statements from part 1 to part 2 of the learning phase (no, positive to negative, negative to positive); (h) how they explained this change (if they noticed any; free response); (i) the relative importance of part 1 versus part 2 of the learning phase in learning about Bob's true character (part 1, part 2, same, unsure); and their agreement with the statements that (j) good people can become bad and (k) bad people can become good (using 101-point sliding scales).
These items were not analyzed for this report but are available in the open data.

Items.

Participants were asked to indicate (a) the percentage of positive statements about the experimental target that were true in part 1 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (b) the percentage of negative statements about the experimental target that were true in part 1 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (c) the percentage of positive statements about the experimental target that were true in part 2 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (d) the percentage of negative statements about the experimental target that were true in part 2 of the learning phase (0% to 100%); (e) whether they noticed any change in the valence of the statements about the experimental target from part 1 to part 2 of the learning phase (no, positive to negative, negative to positive); (f) how they explained this change (if they noticed any; free response); (g) the relative importance of part 1 versus part 2 of the learning phase in learning about the experimental target's true character (part 1, part 2, same, unsure); and their rating of the believability of the information about the experimental target (h) presented in part 1 of the learning phase, (i) presented in part 2 of the learning phase, and (j) overall (using 101-point sliding scales).

Participants in the control condition completed only items (a), (b), and (j); participants in the 1 CA condition completed items (a), (b), and (e) through (j); and participants in all other conditions completed all items.
These items were not analyzed for this report but are available in the open data.
